items.title: FATF: 90% of jurisdictions flag cyber-enabled fraud as a major ML risk — virtual assets carry the proceeds from fraud factories
items.summary: Published 24 February 2026 at the FATF February plenary, 'Cyber-Enabled Fraud – Digitalisation and ML/TF/PF Risks' establishes cyber-enabled fraud as a systemic ML driver: 156 of 174 FATF-assessed jurisdictions (90%) identify it as a major money laundering risk. The paper identifies virtual assets as the primary proceeds-transfer mechanism, documents 'fraud factory' typologies including pig-butchering compounds, romance-investment scams, and tech-support fraud, and calls for three priority responses: domestic public-private coordination, international multi-lateral collaboration, and strengthened victim-detection and reporting frameworks.
items.soWhat: FATF's 90% ML-risk designation makes cyber-enabled fraud a mandatory input to any bank's risk-based approach — not a fringe typology but the dominant ML risk by jurisdiction count. Three implications: (1) transaction-monitoring calibration should treat investment-fraud proceeds as a top-tier risk signal, with higher SAR sensitivity on rapid crypto-to-fiat conversion following relationship-investing patterns; (2) the public-private coordination call is a forward indicator — expect supervisory frameworks to require proactive fraud-intelligence sharing with law enforcement, not just retrospective SAR filing (consistent with the DOJ Disruption Week model, see feed-doj-disruption-week-pig-butchering); (3) the 'fraud factory' typology formally unifies the DPRK, CLMN, and pig-butchering items in this feed under a single FATF risk label — these are not isolated threats but instances of a recognised global ML taxonomy now embedded in the FATF standards framework.

items.title: SEC and CFTC issue landmark joint crypto asset classification — five-part token taxonomy ends enforcement-by-litigation era
items.summary: On March 17, 2026, the SEC and CFTC issued a joint interpretive release establishing the first federal taxonomy for crypto assets: digital commodities (CFTC exclusive jurisdiction), digital collectibles, digital tools, payment stablecoins, and digital securities (tokenised securities). The guidance addresses when a non-security crypto asset can become — and cease to be — subject to securities laws through an 'investment contract'. Activities including airdrops, protocol mining, staking and token wrapping are each addressed. The interpretation followed a March 11, 2026 SEC-CFTC Memorandum of Understanding on shared regulatory coordination.
items.soWhat: The five-part taxonomy is the first authoritative basis in US law for classifying crypto assets — ending five years of SEC enforcement-by-litigation that left financial institutions with no clear framework for counterparty risk on crypto holdings. Three direct compliance implications: (1) banks can now tier counterparty and custody risk frameworks against defined asset categories rather than applying blanket conservatism; (2) the investment-contract clarification — that a non-security asset ceases to be one once issuer obligations are fulfilled — requires ongoing classification monitoring, not a one-time call; (3) combined with the GENIUS Act stablecoin framework (already in force), the SEC-CFTC taxonomy completes the core US regulatory classification map, narrowing residual uncertainty to exchange-level jurisdiction questions the CLARITY Act (still pending; see feed-clarity-act-july4-dead) is intended to resolve.

items.title: Ireland's first digital asset NRA in 7 years: crypto rated 'very significant' ML/TF/sanctions risk — 30-point action plan targets CASPs
items.summary: On 18 June 2026, Ireland's Department of Finance published the country's first National Risk Assessment on Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing, and Proliferation Financing in seven years. Crypto-asset service providers are rated as carrying 'very significant' ML, TF, and sanctions evasion risk — a step up from the 2019 assessment, which pre-dated both MiCA and the explosion of stablecoin volumes. Alongside the NRA, a 30-point Action Plan sets implementation timetables: enhanced transaction monitoring and stricter reporting obligations for financial institutions with crypto exposure, new source-of-funds standards for gambling firms accepting crypto by Q2 2027, and tighter inter-agency intelligence sharing between the CBI, An Garda Síochána, and the Revenue Commissioners.
items.soWhat: Ireland is the EU gateway jurisdiction for Coinbase, Circle, Crypto.com, Gemini and other major CASPs passporting across all 27 member states under MiCA — the Central Bank of Ireland is therefore the lead EU AML supervisor for much of the industry's highest-volume activity. The CBI has already shown willingness to act (issuing Ireland's first crypto enforcement fine in 2025); a formal NRA classifying CASPs at 'very significant' ML risk gives it a mandate and evidence base for supervisory escalation. For banks, two direct implications follow: (1) CASPs passporting via Ireland should be treated as subject to intensifying CBI supervisory pressure — any counterparty relationship with a CBI-regulated CASP should be reassessed using the 30-point action plan as a forward indicator of supervisory expectations; (2) the source-of-funds gambling provision signals that Irish regulators are alive to the CLMN/pig-butchering proceeds corridor through gambling cash-out platforms — a known laundering typology (see feed-chinese-mln-laas-typology).

items.title: CLARITY Act July 4 target confirmed dead — ethics talks collapse and Senate passage probability drops to 45%
items.summary: Closed-door bipartisan negotiations on the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act collapsed in mid-June 2026. The White House withdrew a compromise provision that would have allowed state attorneys general to enforce ethics rules tied to presidential crypto holdings — the condition Democratic holdouts (including Senators Alsobrooks, Gallego, and Gillibrand) had set for floor votes. The White House's July 4 signing target is confirmed logistically impossible. Prediction markets repriced passage probability from above 70% to approximately 45%. Senator Lummis warned that failure to pass before August recess risks deferring final enactment to 2027; the bill needs 60 cloture votes and faces a 31-session-day Senate calendar before recess.
items.soWhat: The CLARITY Act's passage timeline is now genuinely uncertain, not merely delayed. Two direct bank planning implications: (1) the SEC/CFTC exchange-level jurisdiction ambiguity will not be resolved before summer recess — compliance strategies premised on CLARITY Act clarity by Q3 2026 should rebase to a Q4 2026/Q1 2027 base case with meaningful no-passage risk; (2) the ethics-provision resolution — not the Senate calendar — is the leading indicator to monitor: a fresh ethics compromise takes weeks to stabilise after a collapse, so track whether the White House and Democratic holdouts re-engage rather than watching floor scheduling. items.title: Federal Reserve issues GENIUS Act CIP proposed rule — Warsh abstains, secondary-market gap persists, 60-day comment period pushes past July 18 deadline
items.summary: On 18 June 2026, the Federal Reserve Board approved — 5 to 0 with incoming Chair Kevin Warsh abstaining — a proposed rule requiring certain permitted payment stablecoin issuers (PPSIs) to maintain effective customer identification programmes (CIPs) under the Bank Secrecy Act. The proposal requires verification of customer name, birthdate, and address, and screening against US government watchlists. Decentralised protocols are explicitly exempt. Governor Michael Barr voted in favour but flagged a residual gap: the GENIUS Act framework does not adequately address illicit-finance risks in secondary market transactions in payment stablecoins. The 60-day public comment period means the final rule will arrive well after the GENIUS Act's July 18, 2026 implementing-rule statutory deadline.
items.soWhat: The Fed's rule closes the last institutional gap in the GENIUS Act CIP architecture — completing a five-agency suite (OCC, FDIC, NCUA, FinCEN/OFAC, Fed). Three bank compliance implications: (1) BHC-subsidiary stablecoin issuers now face the highest compliance bar of any PPSI pathway — Fed supervision plus bank-equivalent CIP obligations make Fed-supervised issuers the most credible counterparty tier for AML purposes; update counterparty risk tiering to distinguish Fed-supervised PPSIs from OCC-chartered and state-licensed peers. (2) The 60-day comment period (closing mid-August) means the Fed's final rule will land on the January 18, 2027 backstop date, not the accelerated November 2026 scenario; the multi-agency effective-date map is now split. (3) Warsh's unexplained abstention from Powell's proposal — the first meaningful Fed GENIUS Act split — introduces genuine uncertainty about the final rule's scope; track whether Warsh signals preference for supervisory flexibility (lighter CIP for non-bank PPSIs) or Barr's secondary-market extension during the comment period. items.title: FATF June 2026 Plenary: seventh VA/VASP standards update approved, DeFi ML risks report commissioned, UK assumes presidency
items.summary: The sixth and final FATF Plenary under Mexico's presidency (Paris, 17–19 June 2026) approved a seventh targeted update on implementation of the FATF Standards on Virtual Assets and VASPs — to be published July 2026. (2) The UK assuming the FATF Presidency while simultaneously opening its crypto authorisation gateway in September 2026 creates direct structural alignment between FCA's supervisory rulebook and the FATF standards-setting agenda. Expect the UK presidency to prioritise DeFi ML risks and stablecoin issuer obligations as flagship themes — the commissioned DeFi report is the first FATF work specifically on DeFi ML/TF/PF risks; track its publication (July–August 2026 estimate) as a forward indicator of FCA and AMLA supervisory expectations. items.title: Binance confirmed EU exit July 1 — Greece rejects MiCA licence, world's largest exchange loses EU market

items.title: G7 Évian declares DPRK crypto theft a global security threat — $6.75B cumulative, coordinated disruption mandated

items.title: FCA PS26/7: UK authorised funds green-lit to tokenise on DLT — MLR cryptoasset registration required for public blockchain use
items.summary: On 30 April 2026, the FCA published Policy Statement PS26/7 'Progressing Fund Tokenisation', finalising guidance enabling authorised fund managers to use distributed ledger technology (DLT) within the existing regulatory framework. The rules enable the industry Blueprint model for tokenised UK UCITS and non-UCITS schemes, add Handbook guidance for maintaining unitholder registers on DLT, and introduce an optional Direct-to-Fund (D2F) model allowing investors to deal directly with a fund — bypassing the traditional custodian intermediary layer. The FCA authorised the UK's first tokenised UCITS scheme in January 2025. Critically, firms using public DLT networks must implement robust AML controls and may need Money Laundering Regulations registration as a cryptoasset custodian wallet provider until the FSMA cryptoasset regime takes effect in October 2027.
items.soWhat: PS26/7 opens a live regulatory pathway for tokenised UK funds at scale — and explicitly links it to crypto AML obligations. Three bank compliance implications: (1) Banks acting as sub-custodians, depositaries or distributors for tokenised UCITS/NURS products must assess whether the DLT-register function triggers MLR cryptoasset registration now and FSMA cryptoasset permissions from 2027 — the D2F model removes a traditional custodial AML checkpoint, creating new activity and registration exposure. (2) The D2F model bypasses the traditional custodian intermediary layer: banks receiving D2F subscriptions or redemptions must assess whether fund-level investor KYC is sufficient or whether supplementary account-level checks are required, particularly for retail-facing tokenised products. (3) Combined with the cETN 10% cap in CP26/17 (see feed-fca-cp26-17-cetns-authorised-funds) and the FSMA perimeter guidance in CP26/13 (see feed-fca-cp26-13-perimeter-guidance), PS26/7 is the third pillar of a full DLT-in-mainstream-finance rulebook — bank product and compliance teams embedding tokenised assets into fund structures should map all three instruments now rather than at the September 2026 gateway deadline.

items.title: OFAC designates ISIS crypto financing network — Bitcoin Xchange (Syria), Nigerian exchangers and European facilitators; two TRON addresses on SDN
items.summary: On 22 June 2026, OFAC designated three individuals and six entities for facilitating Islamic State (ISIS) terrorist financing via cryptocurrency. At the centre is Bitcoin Xchange — a Syria-based money services business founded by Abdelhakim Boukich (a former Dutch national) — which TRM Labs has tracked since 2022 as a core ISIS crypto off-ramp, with approximately $10 million in traced transactions with ISIS-linked fundraising campaigns. The network connected European donors (Norway, Belgium, Netherlands, France, South Africa, US) transmitting crypto via Telegram channels to Syria-based cash exchangers, who converted funds for ISIS beneficiaries at 2–5% fees. Additional designated entities include three Nigerian bureau de change operators (Nine to Nine Exchange, Manhattan Bureau de Change, Generation Currency Bureau de Change) and individual facilitators Abdurrahmane Miloud (France) and Mukhtar Adamu Muhammad (Nigeria). Two TRON wallet addresses attributed to Miloud were added to the SDN list — among the comparatively rare OFAC actions identifying individual on-chain TRON wallet addresses.
items.soWhat: Three bank compliance steps: (1) add the two designated TRON wallet addresses to blockchain analytics screening feeds immediately — any transaction touching these addresses is a potential sanctions breach. (2) The Telegram-to-Syria-exchanger-to-cash typology differs from Russia/Iran stablecoin-evasion patterns: crypto is used as a cross-border transmission rail to conflict zones, not a store of value, and the off-ramp is informal cash exchange — meaning detection depends on TRON transaction monitoring and Telegram-linked wallet cluster analysis rather than CASP-level screening. (3) The European facilitator angle — French and Dutch nationals routing funds from Western Europe — confirms that retail banking customers, not just specialist crypto businesses, can be network nodes. CTF SAR obligations apply to UK and EU banks whose retail customers transact with designated addresses or entities. The $10M attribution is a known-low estimate based on traced campaign flows; actual ISIS financing routed through this network is likely higher.

items.title: DOJ seizes Huione Group cloud infrastructure in Operation Riptide — $70B CLMN marketplace backbone physically dismantled
items.summary: On 23 June 2026, the Justice Department seized the cloud computing account hosting backend infrastructure for Huione Guarantee (Haowang Guarantee), subsidiaries of Cambodia-based Huione Group. The cloud account ran the marketplace systems that allegedly processed transfers of pig-butchering proceeds, DPRK Lazarus Group cyber-heist funds, and other criminal crypto flows, and facilitated conversion into the legitimate banking sector. Chainalysis estimates the Huione ecosystem processed over $70 billion in crypto transactions across five years; FinCEN's October 2025 Section 311 analysis found at least $4 billion in verifiable illicit proceeds between 2021–2025. The critical compliance implication is that dismantling Huione has not disrupted the CLMN ecosystem — Xinbi Guarantee (which processed $19.9B before its UK designation, migrating to SafeW and XinbiPay) remains the active successor. Banks should not treat the Huione seizure as resolving CLMN exposure: the CLMN operational model survives by migrating platforms, and effective screening requires cluster-level analytics covering Xinbi/SafeW wallet infrastructure, not entity-list matching on Huione alone. The Section 311 prohibition means any residual Huione-linked correspondent or payment flow is a live US sanctions breach.

items.title: FinCEN extends Huione Group Section 311 special measure to H-Pay successor — rebrand loophole closed, 'any successor entity' covered
items.summary: On 25 June 2026, FinCEN published a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (Federal Register 2026-12794) amending the definition of 'Huione Group' in its existing Section 311 special measure to explicitly include H-Pay Service PLC and 'any successor entity.' FinCEN found that Huione Pay PLC — covered by the October 2025 Huione Group Section 311 action severing the network from the US financial system — had rebranded as H-Pay Service PLC to evade public scrutiny and circumvent the measure. The NPRM maintains the same prohibition on US financial institutions: no correspondent accounts or US-dollar payments on behalf of H-Pay. The action is coordinated with OFAC's June 23 second-wave Prince Group designations (9 individuals, 26 entities, including Hu Xiaowei arrested in Osaka on June 14) and the DOJ's Operation Riptide seizure of Huione cloud infrastructure.
items.soWhat: FinCEN's explicit coverage of 'any successor entity' sets a binding precedent: Section 311 special measures now follow rebrand evasion, not just the named legal entity. items.title: No code bug required: governance capture and flash-loan vault-accounting manipulation drain $26M from BonkDAO and Summer.fi in 48 hours
items.summary: Two DeFi protocols were drained on 6 July 2026 using techniques that exploit a protocol's own rules rather than a smart-contract bug. An attacker spent roughly $4M buying BONK to acquire outsized voting power, then passed a malicious BonkDAO governance proposal — live for six days and decided by just seven voting wallets, over 99% of which were attacker-controlled — that authorised transfer of 4.426 billion BONK (~$20M) from the DAO treasury; no timelock, quorum minimum or multisig check existed to stop it. Separately, Summer.fi's Lazy Summer USDC vaults lost roughly $6M after an attacker took an approximately $65.4M flash loan (sourced via Morpho) to manipulate Curve DAI/USDC pool pricing and vault share-accounting, briefly showing a 2.08 million% displayed APY, before converting the proceeds to DAI.

Detection should be extended to cover (1) large token purchases immediately preceding governance votes on low-turnout DAOs — a buy-the-vote pattern distinct from conventional market manipulation, and (2) rapid post-flash-loan stablecoin conversions from lending/vault protocols landing in retail or OTC-facing accounts. Treasury-governance design (timelocks, quorum floors, multisig gates) is becoming a due-diligence criterion in its own right when assessing DeFi-adjacent counterparties or collateral.

items.title: White-hat disclosure: Aptos Move VM bug put an estimated $70bn in cross-chain and stablecoin value at systemic risk
items.summary: Security firm Hexens disclosed on 4 July 2026 that it had privately reported a stale-cache/type-confusion flaw in the Aptos Move VM on 25 February; Aptos Labs patched it within days (27 February), before any exploitation occurred. Hexens simulated the attack using roughly a third of the validator network for about $3,000 and achieved a greater-than-90% success rate; it assessed first-order systemic exposure — value reachable via bridges, cross-chain messaging, stablecoin administration flows and centralised exchanges built on Aptos — at approximately $70bn, though independent verifier Grego AI put directly-at-risk native TVL closer to $250m.
items.soWhat: No funds were lost and the flaw was never exploited, but the gap between $250m of direct exposure and $70bn of first-order systemic exposure is the number worth remembering: a chain-level infrastructure bug can cascade through bridges and stablecoin rails far beyond a protocol's own TVL. Where any part of a digital-asset stack settles on or bridges through a given L1, validator/VM-level vulnerability disclosures belong in counterparty and custody due diligence as a distinct risk category from smart-contract exploits.

items.title: Alfa-Bank moves to build regulated crypto custody in Russia — a sanctioned bank formalising a domestic digital-asset rail

items.title: Interpol's Operation First Light 2026: 5,811 arrests, $293m intercepted across 97 countries — but crypto still outruns the payment-blocking tools
items.summary: Interpol announced results on 9 July 2026 for Operation First Light 2026, a social-engineering-fraud and money-laundering crackdown run 15 January–30 April 2026 across 97 countries with 15,606 suspects identified, 5,811 arrests, USD 293m in illicit assets intercepted, 31,014 bank accounts blocked and 142,000 victims identified. The operation was funded by China's Ministry of Public Security with ASEANAPOL, GCCPOL and Europol support. In one Thailand case, a single wallet processed over USD 122.5m in ten months of romance-scam proceeds using cross-chain token swaps to obscure the trail; Interpol's I-GRIP payment-blocking mechanism successfully froze a linked USD 6.6m business-email-compromise transfer between Singapore and Oman.
items.soWhat: I-GRIP works well against traditional bank-rail transfers but the flagship crypto example in Interpol's own case file — a $122.5m wallet laundered via cross-chain swaps — shows the mechanism has no equivalent reach once proceeds go on-chain. Banks should treat cross-chain bridge/swap sequences following a large single-wallet inflow as a standing red flag for romance-scam proceeds, and expect Interpol/FIU stop-payment requests to keep missing crypto-routed fraud unless matched with blockchain-analytics tooling on the receiving side.

items.title: ICIJ investigation and Wisconsin criminal complaint expose a 30x gap between Tether's and Circle's stolen-fund freeze rates
items.summary: An ICIJ investigation published 8 July 2026 details how Circle rebuffed repeated law-enforcement efforts to recover stolen USDC. In the underlying case, a Walworth County, Wisconsin romance-scam victim sent roughly 381,000 USDC to a fake investment platform; after Milwaukee County detectives obtained an August 2025 court order requiring Circle to freeze the tokens and reissue an equivalent amount to the sheriff's office, Circle refused, saying it lacks the technical ability to burn and reissue USDC held in a third party's wallet — prompting an unusual criminal complaint from Wisconsin prosecutors. AMLBot data cited in the reporting shows Tether froze roughly $3.3bn in USDT across 7,200+ wallets between 2023 and 2025, versus roughly $109m in USDC frozen by Circle over the same period — a 30x gap by value. Circle maintains it acts only on valid legal orders and disputes it profits from leaving frozen assets untouched.
items.soWhat: Issuer-freeze capability — the control this feed has repeatedly flagged as the key sanctions/recovery lever (see feed-t3-fcu-450m-frozen, feed-ofac-cbi-tether-freeze) — is not uniform across major USD stablecoins. Do not assume USDC-denominated fraud or sanctions proceeds will be recovered as readily or as fast as USDT: build the court-order dependency and Circle's slower historical freeze rate into stablecoin counterparty risk tiering, customer victim-recovery expectations, and any product decision that relies on issuer cooperation as a compensating control.

items.title: Russia's crypto foreign-trade payments law takes effect — a state-licensed settlement corridor outside SWIFT
items.summary: On 1 July 2026 Russia's law permitting cryptocurrency (Bitcoin and stablecoins) for cross-border trade settlement came into force, converting a 2024 pilot into statute. Only eight licensed venues may handle the trade; the corridor is narrowly scoped to cross-border invoicing (oil, metals, grain); the ruble remains Russia's sole domestic currency; and transfers above a reporting threshold (reported as low as 60,000 rubles, roughly $800) must be disclosed to the Central Bank and Rosfinmonitoring. Crypto-facilitated trade from Russia reached an estimated 1 trillion rubles (~$11bn) in 2025.
items.soWhat: This formalises a state-licensed, Western-correspondent-independent settlement rail for Russian trade, sitting alongside the A7A5 stablecoin and Alfa-Bank's custody build-out as parallel Russian financial infrastructure (see feed-a7a5-certik-110b-volume, feed-alfabank-russia-crypto-custody). Screen for the eight newly licensed Russian trade venues and treat any counterparty flow touching them as equivalent to direct Russia sanctions exposure — the ruble-denominated reporting regime gives Western institutions no visibility into these flows.

items.title: Circle wins final OCC approval for a national trust bank — USDC reserve custody moves toward direct federal oversight
items.summary: On 10 July 2026 the OCC granted Circle final approval to establish First National Digital Currency Bank, N.A. The charter initially covers fiduciary digital-asset custody for Circle and its affiliates, and is designed to eventually let Circle bring management of the USDC reserve itself under direct federal banking supervision rather than through commercial-bank custodians.
items.soWhat: A federally chartered custodian for USDC's own reserves changes the counterparty-risk calculus for USDC relative to issuers that rely on third-party commercial banks — it is a stronger regulatory assurance than a state money-transmitter licence alone, and a template other stablecoin issuers will likely pursue as GENIUS Act rules finalise. Track whether reserve custody actually migrates into Circle National Trust before treating it as a materially stronger control; the charter itself doesn't yet reduce custodian-concentration risk until reserves move.

items.title: Brazil's Operation Veil of Maya: 87 shell companies used to launder illegal-betting proceeds abroad via crypto
items.summary: On 10 July 2026 Brazil's Federal Police executed nine simultaneous search-and-seizure warrants across São Paulo, Ribeirão Preto, Porto Alegre and Canoas targeting a laundering network built on 87 shell companies. Fiat proceeds from illegal betting entered the shell-company layer, were converted to cryptocurrency, and exited Brazil digitally, leaving a cross-border paper trail that was difficult to follow. Brazil's Finance Ministry and its Prizes and Betting Secretariat supplied the intelligence behind the raids; suspects face potential money-laundering, tax-evasion and organised-crime charges. It follows Operation Exchange five days earlier (5 July), in which the same force dismantled a roughly $2bn crypto laundering ring tied to the PCC (see feed-ofac-pcc-brazil-crypto-laundering).
items.soWhat: Shell-company layering ahead of crypto conversion is now a standing Brazilian laundering pattern for illegal-gambling proceeds, not an isolated case — two coordinated Federal Police operations in five days. Banks with Brazilian corporate-account exposure should treat rapid fiat-to-crypto conversion following inflows from newly formed, thinly staffed corporate entities as a red flag, and cross-reference beneficiary companies against Brazilian gambling and organised-crime enforcement disclosures as they emerge.

items.title: Bank of Thailand and SEC launch joint data-analytics audit of high-volume USDT trading
items.summary: Reported 13 July 2026: the Bank of Thailand and the Thai SEC, working with the Anti-Money Laundering Office, began using data-analytics tools to audit high-volume stablecoin transactions, specifically USDT, for patterns consistent with illicit finance. Preliminary reviews have already surfaced transactions that appear structured to evade disclosure requirements or bypass normal transfer systems. BOT Governor Vitai Ratanakorn framed it as part of a broader Q4 2026 AML push that will also require source-of-funds verification on cash deposits above 5 million baht (~$153,000) and monitoring of gold and large-banknote transactions; no enforcement actions have been announced. A baht-backed stablecoin framework is separately due for public consultation before end-2026.
items.soWhat: A major USDT trading jurisdiction is standing up direct, analytics-driven surveillance of stablecoin flows rather than relying on exchange-level KYC alone — a template other APAC regulators are likely to follow. Banks with Thai corporate or correspondent exposure should treat abnormal high-volume USDT flows through Thai counterparties as an elevated-risk signal now, ahead of any formal enforcement action landing.

items.title: China's top prosecutors propose treating mixer or privacy-coin use as presumptive proof of money-laundering intent
items.summary: A paper published 13 July 2026 on the Supreme People's Procuratorate's official website, co-authored by two SPP officials and a Xiangtan University professor, calls for a fundamental shift in how Chinese investigators build crypto money-laundering cases. It proposes presuming criminal intent when a suspect uses a mixer, transacts in privacy coins, or sells crypto at off-market prices, unless they can produce 'reasonable counter-evidence' — and would make on-chain records and analytics-firm reports admissible evidence outright. It also calls for a national platform to hold and liquidate seized crypto, a gap created by China's own trading ban.
items.soWhat: This is a burden-of-proof inversion, not a guidance update: mixer or privacy-coin use alone becomes the evidentiary trigger rather than one red flag among many. It also runs directly counter to the more nuanced US Treasury line on mixers having legitimate privacy uses (see feed-treasury-genius-innovation-report) — a live regulatory divergence to track for any China-nexus flows. For counterparties or corridors touching Chinese-linked wallets, treat any mixer or privacy-coin hop as a materially harder-to-defend exposure going forward, and watch whether analytics-firm attribution reports start being cited as admissible evidence elsewhere.

Track admissibility of blockchain-analytics-firm reports as a precedent for other jurisdictions

items.soWhat: Enforcement is moving up the ransomware supply chain — sanctioning the VPNs and cryptor tools that keep malware undetected, and syndicate leadership, not just cash-out wallets. Extend sanctions screening to the enabling-service layer (VPN/cryptor vendors, high-risk exchanges like Cryptomus) and treat historical exposure to Stern/TrickBot-linked wallets as a live SDN/EU-list hit rather than a legacy Conti-era concern.

items.title: FATF's 7th targeted update: stablecoins now dominate illicit VA volume, and criminal groups are launching their own freeze-resistant tokens
items.summary: Published 16 July 2026, FATF's seventh targeted update on implementation of its virtual-asset/VASP standards finds most identified on-chain illicit activity now involves stablecoins, and documents a Cambodia-based financial-services conglomerate that laundered at least $4bn (2021-2025) for both organised-crime fraud rings and DPRK cyber-theft through shared infrastructure — after a legitimate issuer froze $29m of the group's tokens, it launched its own proprietary stablecoin marketed as freeze-resistant. Separately, a Spanish network laundered roughly €460m from over 5,000 fraud victims. Travel Rule implementation among surveyed jurisdictions rose to 83% (from 73% a year earlier), though FATF says enforcement remains uneven; jurisdictions with materially important VA activity now cover about 97% of the global market.
items.soWhat: Issuer-freeze capability, the control this feed has repeatedly flagged as the key sanctions lever (see feed-ofac-cbi-tether-freeze, feed-fatf-stablecoin-report), now has a documented counter-typology: criminal groups standing up their own stablecoins specifically to evade it, mirroring the A7A5 kill-switch-free design already tracked. Add 'proprietary/house stablecoin with no freeze function, tied to an offshore payments conglomerate' as a standing red flag in vendor and counterparty stablecoin due diligence, not just sanctioned-issuer screening.

items.title: DPRK hides crypto-wallet-stealing malware in fake coding tests and poisoned npm packages
items.summary: Two North Korea-linked developer-targeting campaigns surfaced in July 2026. Elastic Security Labs disclosed on 17 July that the DPRK-aligned 'Contagious Interview' cluster (tracked as REF9403) now hides malicious payloads inside SVG 'flag' images in fake job-application coding-test repositories; running the trojanised project drops a four-stage OtterCookie-aligned toolkit — a browser/crypto-wallet credential stealer, a file stealer, a Socket.IO remote-access trojan and a clipboard stealer. Separately, JFrog reported on 3 July that six npm packages masquerading as Rollup polyfills (including 'rollup-packages-polyfill-core' and 'quirky-token') delivered a two-stage payload — overlapping with the known OtterCookie/BeaverTail malware families and linked to prior Lazarus Group activity — that harvested browser and cryptocurrency-wallet credentials, SSH keys, AWS tokens and clipboard data from developer workstations.
items.soWhat: DPRK's crypto-theft pipeline now reaches upstream of the blockchain entirely — compromising a developer's machine via a fake recruiting lure or a poisoned open-source package yields wallet keys and cloud credentials before any on-chain transaction happens. Any counterparty or vendor whose engineers could be targeted (crypto-native firms, custody providers, DeFi protocols the bank has exposure to) should be asked about developer-endpoint controls and npm/software-supply-chain vetting, not just smart-contract audits; threat-intel/wallet-attribution feeds should also flag OtterCookie/BeaverTail-linked infrastructure as a precursor signal for compromised-key laundering.

items.title: CertiK: wallet compromise overtakes smart-contract bugs as Web3's costliest attack vector, $1.3bn stolen in H1 2026
items.summary: CertiK's Hack3D H1 2026 report, published 17 July 2026, recorded roughly $1.32bn in Web3 losses across 344 incidents (up about 28% year-on-year excluding the 2025 Bybit baseline). Wallet compromise was the single costliest category — over $444m across just 33 incidents, driven by private-key, multisig-governance and operational-security failures rather than code bugs (which cost $151.6m). items.soWhat: 'Audited' is an increasingly incomplete signal of protocol safety: due-diligence questionnaires for DeFi and custody counterparties should weight key-custody, multisig operational security and signer-permission hygiene at least as heavily as smart-contract audit history, since operational/key failures now cause more loss than code vulnerabilities.

items.title: GENIUS Act's one-year rulemaking deadline passes 18 July with no final stablecoin rules from any of the six agencies
items.summary: The statutory 18 July 2026 deadline this feed flagged in advance (see feed-genius-act-six-agency-july18-deadline) has now passed: none of OFAC, FinCEN, the Federal Reserve, OCC, FDIC or NCUA finalised permitted-payment-stablecoin-issuer rules in time. Key comment periods run past the deadline itself — the OCC's AML rule closes 24 July, the FDIC's compliance framework 4 August, and a five-agency customer-identification rule 21 August — so a coordinated final package was not realistically possible. The GENIUS Act's statute has no fallback or interim-guidance mechanism for a missed deadline. Separately, reporting on Tether's most recent disclosures flags that roughly a quarter of USDT's reserves still sit in assets (precious metals, lending positions, bitcoin holdings) that would not meet GENIUS's cash-and-Treasuries reserve standard, even before any compliance deadline bites for non-US issuers.
items.soWhat: 'GENIUS-Act-compliant issuer' is not yet a real category — banks should not treat any PPSI as operating under a finalised federal AML/sanctions framework, and should hold a contingency view that the rule set lands piecemeal through late 2026 or into 2027 rather than as a clean cutover. For non-US issuers such as Tether specifically, the reserve-composition gap is a second, independent readiness question distinct from the rulemaking delay — worth tracking separately in stablecoin counterparty due diligence rather than assuming resolution once US rules do land.

It follows the MiCA transitional period's 1 July expiry and a CASP register that has grown past 280 authorised providers.

items.title: AMLA chair warns post-MiCA customer migration could strain CASP AML compliance
items.summary: Speaking to the European Parliament's ECON committee around 15 July 2026, AMLA chair Bruna Szego warned that the 1 July MiCA transitional-period cutoff is driving a wave of customers from unlicensed platforms toward licensed VASPs, and that this migration could strain those firms' AML compliance capacity — onboarding large new customer volumes quickly risks weakening controls even at properly authorised providers. Szego confirmed AMLA will publish a full report assessing crypto-sector money-laundering risk and cross-member-state supervisory consistency before year-end, and said AMLA is expanding its own blockchain-analytics and tracing capability.
items.soWhat: A licensed CASP absorbing a large post-MiCA customer influx is not automatically a lower-risk counterparty during the migration window itself — banks relying on MiCA authorisation as a due-diligence proxy should ask licensed EU CASP counterparties specifically how onboarding surge capacity and KYC/CDD controls are holding up in H2 2026, rather than treating the licence as a static assurance, and should flag AMLA's year-end report as a near-term primary source to revisit.

items.title: Wanchain's Cardano-BNB Chain bridge drained of ~$10m via signature-reuse flaw in four transactions
items.summary: On 21 July 2026, an attacker exploited Wanchain's cross-chain bridge connecting Cardano to BNB Chain, stealing roughly 515.2 million NIGHT tokens (Midnight, the Cardano-incubated chain) worth about $10m across four transactions completed within eight minutes. The root cause was a non-injective signed-message encoding flaw in the bridge's TreasuryCheck validator: 14 variable-length fields were raw-concatenated without delimiters or length prefixes, so different field combinations could produce identical byte strings, enabling signature reuse that inflated authorised withdrawal amounts roughly 65,000x. Wanchain confirmed the incident and paused the bridge pending investigation.
items.soWhat: Another entry in the recurring cross-chain-bridge exploit pattern this feed tracks (see feed-defi-governance-accounting-exploits-july2026, feed-ostium-oracle-exploit-2026): bridge validator logic remains a favoured laundering-adjacent attack surface because stolen funds move instantly across chains before monitoring catches up. Reinforces treating bridge-mediated transfers as elevated-risk in any transaction-monitoring policy, not just mixer or privacy-coin flows.

items.title: FATF publishes DeFi report: 'decentralised' platforms routinely have identifiable controllers, but 132 of 142 jurisdictions still haven't applied VASP rules to them
items.summary: On 21 July 2026 FATF published its Targeted Report on Regulatory Challenges from Decentralised Finance, updating its 2021 DeFi guidance. The report finds that platforms marketed as decentralised routinely retain identifiable controlling parties — developers, governance-token holders, front-end operators — who meet the FATF definition of a VASP, and sets out indicators for testing 'control' in practice. Despite this, 132 of 142 surveyed jurisdictions have not implemented the Recommendation 15 standard for qualifying DeFi arrangements, and only two jurisdictions have actually licensed or registered one.
items.soWhat: This closes the loop flagged when the FATF plenary commissioned the report in June (see feed-fatf-june-plenary-defi-va-update). It gives banks a concrete due-diligence lens: apply FATF's 'who has control' test — deploy rights, admin keys, fee capture, governance-token concentration — to any DeFi protocol counterparty, on the working assumption that it will be treated as an unlicensed VASP in roughly 93% of jurisdictions regardless of its decentralisation claims. Expect this control test to surface next in FCA, AMLA and GENIUS Act DeFi guidance.

items.title: Russia's Duma passes comprehensive crypto law — bitcoin as property, sanctions-bypass trade legalised, Sberbank and VTB building custody rails
items.summary: On 21 July 2026 Russia's State Duma passed the final readings of Bill No. 1194918-8, 'On Digital Currency and Digital Rights' — the country's first comprehensive crypto statute, distinct from the narrower cross-border trade-payments law already in force since 1 July (feed-russia-crypto-foreign-trade-law-july2026). It classifies bitcoin and other crypto as property under the civil code rather than currency, formally legalises crypto in foreign trade while keeping domestic payments banned, caps non-qualified retail investors at 300,000 rubles (roughly $3,800) a year under central-bank oversight, and licenses exchanges, brokers and custodians. Core provisions take effect 1 September 2026, with unlicensed platforms banned from 1 July 2027, pending Federation Council approval and Putin's signature — both considered formalities. Sberbank, VTB, T-Bank Group and the Moscow Exchange have already announced custody, depository and trading infrastructure timed to the law.
items.soWhat: State-owned banks building licensed crypto rails ahead of a law explicitly designed to keep sanctions-bypass trade legal while banning domestic use is a second, parallel plank of Russian sanctions-evasion infrastructure alongside A7A5 and the July 1 trade corridor (see feed-a7a5-certik-110b-volume, feed-russia-crypto-foreign-trade-law-july2026). Treat any correspondent, liquidity or CASP exposure touching Sberbank, VTB or Moscow Exchange crypto products from September onward as direct Russia sanctions-nexus exposure, not generic crypto counterparty risk.

items.title: EU ambassadors agree the 21st Russia sanctions package six weeks late — 11 crypto platforms and roughly 90 banks now cut off
items.summary: On 22 July 2026, six weeks after being unveiled on 10 June, EU ambassadors reached political agreement on the 21st Russia sanctions package, with formal legal adoption to follow. It bars EU persons from transacting with 11 named crypto platforms and roughly 90-94 Russian banks and financial institutions, and retains the European Commission's power to designate entire third countries as off-limits for crypto-asset services if found to be hosting Russian sanctions-evasion platforms. The final bank count is lower than the 100+ figure floated in June, reflecting a package described by reporting as 'watered down' after weeks of member-state negotiation.
items.soWhat: Same country-level kill-switch mechanism already flagged (feed-eu-russia-21st-sanctions-country-ban) — the six-week gap between proposal and agreement confirms this class of measure now moves on political rather than technical timelines. Banks screening for the 11 platforms and the intermediary-jurisdiction risk (Turkey, UAE, Kazakhstan, Hong Kong) should not wait for the Official Journal text to start counterparty review; track formal legal adoption, expected shortly, for the final entity list.

items.title: EU's 21st Russia sanctions package formally adopted — crypto platform count rises to 14, four separate A7/A7A5 designations, new third-country crypto ban power
items.summary: On 24 July 2026 the EU formally adopted the 21st Russia sanctions package agreed in principle two days earlier. The final legal text lists 14 crypto-asset service platforms (up from the 11 floated on 22 July), based in Georgia, Panama, the UAE, the Marshall Islands, Kyrgyzstan and Belarus, and adds four separate designations targeting the A7 cross-border payments network and its A7A5 rouble-pegged stablecoin, which Chainalysis data cited in reporting puts at close to $120bn in processed volume. The package also creates a new instrument letting the EU impose a full third-country ban on crypto-asset services where a jurisdiction is found to host Russian sanctions-evasion platforms.
items.soWhat: This is the formal adoption the prior entry (feed-eu-21st-sanctions-package-agreed-july2026) flagged as pending — the entity list grew between political agreement and legal text, so counterparty screening built off the 22 July figure (11 platforms) is now stale; refresh against the adopted 14-platform list. The new third-country-ban instrument is the more consequential change for ongoing monitoring: it lets the EU cut off an entire jurisdiction's crypto sector rather than designating platforms one by one, so a bank's intermediary-jurisdiction risk list (Georgia, UAE, Kyrgyzstan and similar) should be treated as a single watch-list, not case-by-case exposure.

items.title: Three DeFi exploits in one day — AFX Trade, Verus and B² Network lose $35.55m combined, again via bridge infrastructure
items.summary: On 23 July 2026 three separate protocols were exploited within hours of each other: AFX Trade (a decentralised perpetuals exchange on Arbitrum) lost $24.15m to a vulnerable third-party bridge integration, Verus's Ethereum bridge lost $7.55m, and B² Network lost $3.86m — a combined $35.55m. Arbitrum's co-founder confirmed the native Arbitrum bridge itself was not compromised; the AFX Trade exploiter bridged the stolen funds to Ethereum and swapped them into ETH. AFX Trade has offered its exploiter a white-hat deal (keep 30%, return the rest).
items.soWhat: A fourth cluster of bridge-mediated DeFi losses inside two weeks (see feed-wanchain-cardano-bnb-bridge-exploit, feed-defi-governance-accounting-exploits-july2026, feed-ostium-oracle-exploit-2026) confirms third-party bridge integrations, not base-layer bridges, are the recurring weak point. Any DeFi counterparty due-diligence should separately score a protocol's own contracts versus the bridges and integrations it depends on — a clean audit of the former says nothing about the latter.

items.title: FinCEN Director Gacki faces House oversight hearing — beneficial-ownership rule 'very close' to finalised, crypto enforcement posture questioned
items.summary: On 21 July 2026 the House Financial Services Subcommittee on National Security, Illicit Finance and International Financial Institutions held an oversight hearing on FinCEN operations, with Director Andrea Gacki testifying. Lawmakers pressed Gacki on enforcement priorities and resourcing, including how the agency is approaching emerging financial technologies and cryptocurrency, amid industry concern that aggressive enforcement and unclear guidance could impose disproportionate costs on smaller institutions. Gacki said FinCEN is 'very close to the finish line' on finalising a revised beneficial ownership reporting rule.
items.soWhat: No new rule resulted, but the hearing signals where BSA/AML enforcement pressure is heading: a still-unfinalised beneficial ownership rule creates near-term uncertainty for CTA-linked customer due-diligence programmes, and Congress's explicit framing of crypto alongside 'regulatory complexity' concerns for smaller institutions suggests FinCEN's next crypto-specific guidance may lean toward proportionality rather than a further tightening. Worth tracking for the beneficial-ownership final rule text once published.
